
DI pattern is a specific version of [[Inversion of Control]] (IoC) pattern where implementations of an object are passed into another object through constructors/ setters/ getters/ service lookups, which the object will “depend on” in order to behave correctly.

Simple: https://www.jamesshore.com/v2/blog/2006/dependency-injection-demystified

![](data:image/png;base64,)
(Source: [The 3 Types of Dependency Injection - LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/3-types-dependency-injection-mohammad-ramezani?articleId=6708012950256439296))

## Method 1: Constructor Injection

This is the most common way of implementing DI. It is the process of using the constructor to pass in the dependencies of a class. This method should be used when your class has a dependency that the class requires in order to work properly. Also use this method when the dependency in question has a lifetime longer than a single method. Dependencies passed into the constructor should be useful to the class in a general way, with its use spanning multiple methods in the class. Checking for NULL is necessary and is boilerplate code. If a dependency is used in only one spot, use method injection. 

This method assumes that the entire program is using the pattern, which means the whole system must be refactored at the same time, providing the disadvantages of being time-consuming, difficult, and risky. Easiest method for unit testing.

(Source: [Dependency Injection - techtarget.com](https://www.techtarget.com/searchapparchitecture/definition/dependency-injection?_gl=1*h44747*_ga*MTExNDc0NzY2NC4xNjUxNjk2NzYw*_ga_TQKE4GS5P9*MTY1MTY5Njc1OS4xLjEuMTY1MTY5NjgxMy4w&_ga=2.238519040.1202781024.1651696760-1114747664.1651696760))
(Source: [The 3 Types of Dependency Injection - LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/3-types-dependency-injection-mohammad-ramezani?articleId=6708012950256439296))

## Method 2: Method Injection

Useful when the implementation of a dependency will vary (overloaded dependency constructors) and when the dependency needs to be renewed after each use (dependency needs to update upon manipulation). In both these cases, it’s up to the caller to decide what implementation to pass to the method.

If you have, for example, an interface which has multiple methods which each call different implementations of a dependency, you would use Method Injection to inject the dependency as an argument to each method.

(Source: [The 3 Types of Dependency Injection - LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/3-types-dependency-injection-mohammad-ramezani?articleId=6708012950256439296))

## Method 3: Property Injection

Also known as Setter Injection this method should be used when the dependency is optional. This means the class will be able to function without the dependent class. Dependency can be injected by calling a setter method to assign the argument reference to a member variable. It is important to note that assigning dependency using a setter method means that the dependency will not be injected upon object creation, even if it is called in close succession to object creation.  
  
“Property injection is considered bad in 98% of all scenarios because it hides dependencies and there is no guarantee that the object will be injected when the class is created”.  
  
(Source: [Property Injection in ASP.NET Core - StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/38459625/property-injection-in-asp-net-core))
(Source: [The 3 Types of Dependency Injection - LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/3-types-dependency-injection-mohammad-ramezani?articleId=6708012950256439296))

## Comparison:

|   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|
|DI Method|Constructor|Setter|Method|
|DI Point|Constructor|On method call|On method call|
|Dependency Created|On object creation|On method call|On method call|
|Dependency scope|Class member|Class member|Method scope|
|Best Use|Class requires dependency for functionality|Dependency is optional or limited in use|Multiple implementations of dependency is required|

## Alternative Approach: Service Locator

A Service Locator acts as a singleton registry for all services that are used by your application. There are static and dynamic locators (to support new services).

Decide which interface implementation the locator will return or if you want to use an external configuration parameter that specifies the name of the class that implements the interface. The latter is more flexible but also more complex.

This method offers an alternative to Constructor Injection as it can be implemented slowly, refactoring the application one piece at a time, as is convenient. It is essentially a subset of IoC and not DI (IoC -> Service Locator & DI). DI is usually considered the Best Practice for a project unless there is a specific reason for using Service Locators (one reason being that Service Locators require more sophisticated testing).

A service locator contains references to the services and encapsulates the logic that locates them. In your classes, use the service locator to obtain service instances. The Service Locator pattern does not describe how to instantiate the services. It describes a way to register services and locate them. Typically, the Service Locator pattern is combined with the Factory pattern and/or the Dependency Injection pattern. This combination allows a service locator to create instances of services.

A service locator should be able to locate a service without knowing its concrete type. For example, it might use a string key or a service interface type. This allows you to replace the concrete implementation of the dependency without modifying the classes.  
  
![](data:image/png;base64,)

ClassA depends on Service A and B and is vulnerable to any changes made to these services. If Service A or B undergo changes, ClassA and any ClassX that depends on these services will also require code changes to adapt to the new implementations of their dependencies.  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

ClassA now depends on the locator which intermediates serviceA and B. This way, if Service A or B undergo changes, the locator may be changed but every ClassX which depends on the locator will not require change.

Use the [[Service Locator]] pattern to achieve any of the following objectives:

- Decouple classes from their dependencies so dependencies can be changed with minimal change to the classes.
- Write logic that depends on classes whose concrete implementation isn’t known at compile time.
- Test your classes in isolation, without the dependencies.
- Separate the logic that locates and manages the dependencies from the class
- You want to divide your application into loosely coupled modules that can be independently developed, tested, versioned, and deployed.

One criticism of this method is that this removes the dependency altogether rather than eliminating the tight coupling.

Solution:

- Any module that requires a motor instance will depend instead on a locator
- Remove instance creation within modules
- Modules will use reference to instance instead
- Reference will be provided as an argument to the module (constructor/ setter)
- A request to the locator for the required resource in enum
- Locator will instantiate an object from definition class and provide the reference back to the requesting module.

(Source: [The Service Locator Pattern  - Microsoft Docs](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/msp-n-p/ff648968\(v=pandp.10\)))**
